sections.text: Not every assignment moves. Simple values like integers, floats, bool and char are copied instead. Both variables stay usable.

These types implement Copy, which marks a type as cheap to copy byte for byte. Rust copies them automatically instead of moving them. (Copy is a trait: a trait is a named set of abilities or methods that a type promises to have. Unit 7 covers traits.) Tuples and arrays made only of Copy types are Copy too. String isn't Copy, because it owns text on the heap.
For types like String, ask for a full copy explicitly with .clone():
clone() copies the heap data, which can be slow for big values. That's why Rust makes you write it: you can see where expensive copies happen.
Clone is a good way to get unstuck while you're learning. Later you'll often swap it for a reference, which avoids the copy.
You can add these to your own types with #[derive(Clone, Copy)]. Copy is only allowed when every field is Copy, so a struct containing a String can be Clone but never Copy.

exercise.prompt: first is moved into second, so it can't be printed. Use .clone() so both can be printed. It should print: apple apple

quiz.question: Which of these is copied, not moved, on assignment?
What does .clone() do to a String?
options: Makes a full copy of its data

quiz.question: Why doesn't Rust clone Strings automatically?
options: Cloning can be expensive, so it should be visible
